item.title: Most voters in key states want to block US arms transfers to Israel
item.description:
A majority of likely voters in each of six key swing states — Georgia, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, and Texas — say they approve of measures to block the transfer of bombs to Israel, according to a new poll released Wednesday by the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) and conducted by the YouGov data analytics firm.

The poll also found that majorities or strong pluralities of 3,200 respondents in the six states favor “cutting $3.3 billion in taxpayer-funded weapons to Israel” and believe the war in Iran benefits Israel more than the United States.

As in other recent polls, the new survey, which was conducted from late September to mid-October, found that self-identified Democrats and Independents were significantly more likely to oppose more military transfers to Israel than self-identified Republicans in each state, although at least one-third of Republicans in all of the states except North Carolina (26%) said they supported blocking bombs to Israel.

The highest percentage of Republicans taking that position was found in Maine, where 45% said they opposed more such transfers. Incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who is in a tight race against a Democrat who has criticized U.S. military aid and sales to Israel, voted against a resolution to ban the transfer of 1,000- and 2,000-pound bombs to Israel April 15, the last time the Senate voted on the issue. That vote marked the first time that a majority of Senate Democrats (36 of 46 members of the caucus) voted to block weapons transfers to Israel.

IMEU is a pro-Palestinian organization. YouGov, which fielded the survey, is considered a reliable pollster, and the poll’s questions were posed in neutral terms.

All six of the states polled by YouGov are considered critical to Democratic hopes of gaining control of the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. Of the six Senate seats that are contested in them this year, only one is currently held by a Democrat, Jon Ossoff of Georgia.

The survey suggests that support for Israel and the Iran war among Republicans could prove a liability in next month’s midterm elections. As RS reported last week, some Republican Senate candidates in battleground states have tried to distance themselves from the Iran war, though few have voted in Congress to end or restrict it.

While the survey did not ask respondents how much weight they would accord U.S. military support for Israel and the war in Iran in deciding how they will vote in this year’s senatorial elections, it comes as a series of other polls have shown unprecedented popular disapproval of Israel’s conduct in its three-year-old war in Gaza and persistent strong opposition (55%) to the ongoing U.S. conflict in Iran. A pair of recent polls also indicated that voters are more concerned about the Iran war than immigration or crime, two issues that Republicans tend to dominate.

On whether they approve or disapprove of “Senate measures to block the transfer of bombs to Israel,” 65% of Maine respondents said they approved, while only 22% said they disapproved. In Georgia, the split was 55% approved, and 28% disapproved; in Iowa, the split was 56%-24%; North Carolina, 51%-30%; Ohio, 57%-31%; and Texas 54%-30%.

Asked about “cutting $3.3 billion in taxpayer-funded weapons to Israel” that the U.S. provides each year, 52% of Georgia respondents said they approved, while 34% said they disapproved. In Iowa, the split was 59%-26%; in Maine, 57%-30%; North Carolina, 48%-34%; Ohio, 54%-37%; and Texas, 52%-34%.

Asked which country the Iran war benefits the most, 50% of Georgia voters said Israel, while 28% said the U.S.; in Iowa, the split was 54% Israel, 21% the U.S.; Maine, 59%-19%; North Carolina, 52%-23%; Ohio, 49%-27%; and Texas, 51%-25%.

item.title: What's the point of a permanent US military base in Poland?
item.description:
When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the United States deployed almost 5,000 troops to Poland, doubling the number that had already been stationed there. The reinforcements were sent mostly to southeastern Poland, close to the border with Ukraine, and their task was to deter further Russian aggression.

Warsaw welcomed the move but uncertainty persisted: the troops were deployed on a rotational, not permanent, basis. Now Poland, which prides itself on being the staunchest U.S. ally in Europe, wants more.

For many months, the center-left government and the right-wing presidential administration have been in talks with the Trump administration to set up a permanent U.S. military base in Poland. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk recently said the decision is “imminent” and should be made no later than December, while Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy, wrote that there is an “ongoing exploration of potential opportunities for permanent basing of U.S. forces in Poland.” According to Stanisław Wziątek, another Polish deputy defense minister, the prospective base could accommodate up to 5,000 additional troops.

Details of the negotiations are scarce, but expectations in Poland run high. The government sees the Trump administration’s decision as a test of whether it is willing to put additional pressure on Russia. The presidential administration wants to capitalize on President Karol Nawrocki’s good relations with President Donald Trump to secure a favor in the form of a permanent U.S. military base. Both sides would be massively disappointed should the U.S. eventually pass on the project.

There is reason to believe, however, that the long-awaited base is not as crucial to Poland’s security as officials in Warsaw like to think. The very fact that the talks between Poland and the United States have dragged on for many months suggests that there is little sense of urgency, at least in the White House, and that the threat of Russian attack on Poland is not imminent.

For Poland, this should be a clear indication that the key to its security lies neither in amassing U.S. troops on its territory, nor in currying favor with Trump – who may change his mind at any time – but rather in adopting a more independent-minded attitude, which would allow for more political flexibility and a greater focus on its own military potential.

Russian threat, American retreat


It is true that the Russian drones and fighter jets regularly fly close to the Polish border and occasionally violate Polish airspace. It is also true that Russia has carried out sabotage operations in Poland, according to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk. But there is no serious indication that Moscow intends to, or is able to, invade Poland.

Even if Russia wanted to subjugate Poland, one should bear in mind that since 2022, hundreds of thousands of Russian troops have failed to break through the front lines in the Donbas, a region located more than 600 miles away from the Polish-Ukrainian border. It is also not difficult to figure out that invading Poland would make absolutely no sense for Russian President Vladimir Putin at a time when he is hoping to reach a deal with Trump.

The sluggish pace of U.S.-Polish negotiations stems from the Trump administration’s National Security Strategy. Since the beginning of 2025, the United States has largely focused on reducing its commitments and cutting down the U.S. military presence in Europe, not shoring it up. In December, the Pentagon is expected to conclude its review of the U.S. force posture in Europe, and the most likely result is the reduction in troop levels on the continent. It is plausible that the project of a permanent base in Poland will be scrapped too, or at least put on the shelf. After all, that would be consistent with the Pentagon’s concept of “NATO 3.0,” which aims to shift the responsibility for conventional deterrence to European allies.

There is a possibility, of course, that the White House goes forward with a permanent base in Poland. This would likely reflect a short-term victory by the hawks in the administration and Congress who want to put more pressure on Russia. Alternatively, this could be Trump's gesture toward Nawrocki, a fellow nationalist, whom he praises lavishly. Either way, Polish officials should not delude themselves into thinking that such a decision would be made out of concern for Poland’s security in particular.

Time to change gears


Given these circumstances, Polish officials should think about their country’s security in a more unorthodox and open-minded way. Poland is a dynamic, rapidly-developing economy that needs three things to prosper: physical security, political stability and a high level of investment. There is a serious risk, however, that a protracted “forever” war across the border, coupled with ever-increasing tensions between Russia and Europe, will make it much more difficult to achieve these goals.

The likelihood of such a bleak scenario is all the more probable because Poland now believes that the conflict between Russia and the West is inevitable and that the only way to ensure its own security is through military means. Warsaw heavily invests in military equipment while senior government officials declare that they want to have the largest army in Europe. Poland’s defense budget is approaching 5% of its GDP, and the slogan “if you want peace, prepare for war” can be heard almost everywhere.

But the fact that this militarization occurs in a total absence of European-led diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and ending the war in Ukraine makes Poland more, not less, vulnerable. Officials in Warsaw may not see it this way, but relations between Europe and Russia have steadily been spiraling into the so-called security dilemma, an international relations theory premised on the observation that defensive preparations by one side are almost inevitably viewed as offensive by its enemy. The crux of security dilemma is that no amount of additional equipment or troops can make either side feel safer. Once the downward spiral begins, things can very easily get out of control. And that is exactly what is happening right now.

So what might a new approach to Polish security look like?

In the foreseeable future, military partnership with the United States will remain a bedrock of Polish foreign policy, but from Warsaw’s perspective it would be a mistake to indefinitely rely on American equipment and security guarantees.

In the current geopolitical environment, Poland would be wise to speed up the development of its own military industry, especially in the field of drones, automation and AI. This could make it more resistant to a threat posed by Russia's hybrid operations or any other future threats.

But first and foremost, Poland should recognize an urgent need to invest in an active and flexible diplomacy aimed at reducing hostility and tensions with the country it fears the most.

This would be no easy task, and, most likely, it would not yield any concrete result at the beginning. But it would be a far more prudent path than desperately seeking a permanent U.S. lifeline at a time when the U.S. is pulling back from Europe.

The outcome of the battle for Donbas — and the war itself — hinges on whether Ukraine can hold Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. How are two former Azov commanders leading the defense?
item.description: The Ukrainian command is trying to stop the Russian offensive — the decisive push in the battle for Donbas — on the approaches to the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk urban area. To do this, it has created two operational groupings, both led by veterans of the Azov Brigade: the “Center” grouping, tasked with holding Sloviansk, is commanded by Andriy Biletsky (former commander of the 3rd Army Corps), while the Azov grouping guarding the approaches to Kramatorsk is commanded by Denys Prokopenko (former commander of the 12th National Guard Brigade, which was reconstituted after the 2022 capture of its forces in Mariupol in 2022). Biletsky’s troops have already distinguished themselves with a successful offensive: they pushed Russia’s 20th Army back across the Siverskyi Donets north of Sloviansk, and are now trying to drive back the forces advancing on the city from the east and south. Prokopenko’s task is harder: he took up his new post in the midst of a fresh Russian breakthrough between Dobropillia and Kramatorsk. In this sector, Ukrainian forces are dealing with a full-blown crisis — possibly more serious than the one caused by the Russian breakthrough in the same area 14 months ago. Russian troops have already cut the Dobropillia-Kramatorsk road, are storming the first city, and are pushing toward the outskirts of the second.

item.title: Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030?
item.description:
Why has Egypt’s President Sisi said he will step down in 2030? Expert comment thilton.drupal 22 October 2026

Egyptian president’s surprise announcement comes amid deep economic difficulties and includes a plan for a military-approved succession.

Egypt’s President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi has declared he will step down at the end of his third term in 2030. Speaking during the Egyptian Military Academy graduation on 17 October, he also outlined a military-centric succession process to select the next president and senior officials beyond 2030. 

The statement surprised many observers, and perhaps even state officials. If Sisi follows through on his pledge and leaves peacefully, he’d be the first Egyptian president to leave office without dying, being imprisoned or facing a popular uprising. 

The unprecedented decision will have significant implications for Egypt’s political landscape, the balance of power within the regime and the military’s influence over politics and governance.

Why is Sisi leaving?

Sisi became president in 2014, after the overthrow of Mohamed Morsi’s short-lived Muslim Brotherhood government. He is currently serving his third term, after winning elections seen as predetermined in 2018 and 2023. A constitutional referendum in 2019, also seen as predetermined, increased the president’s term from four to six years, extending Sisi’s current term to 2030.

Sisi, who is 71, did not give an exact reason for why he would step down in his speech at the military academy. He said that there would be no further amendments to Egypt’s constitution to prolong his rule and declared it ‘a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed,’ suggesting a transition of power is inevitable.  

Economic troubles

Two factors likely lie behind this surprise decision. 

First, the debt-financed economic model pursued under Sisi is unsustainable. This system has sustained military dominance and stalled urgent economic reform. The government’s vast borrowing to fund mega projects has created a structural economic crisis. 

In this year’s budget, debt servicing accounts for 63.9 per cent of planned expenditure, a significant increase from 43 per cent in 2014. Interest payments alone, as a share of GDP, exceed the combined allocations for education, healthcare, wages and subsidies combined. Egypt’s external debt rose from $46.1 billion in 2014 (16.4 per cent of GDP) to $164.8 billion (38.9 per cent of GDP) by the end of Q1 2026. 

The Egyptian pound exchange rate has plummeted from 7.14 per dollar in mid-2014 to about 53.8 per dollar in October 2026. Urban inflation has risen from 8.3 per cent in May 2014 to 13.9 per cent in September 2026 and is expected to rise further. 

This increased pressure on ordinary Egyptians has made the last decade one of plummeting living standards. Official data shows the national poverty rate has reached 35.7 per cent in 2023.

Public anger over rising living costs, combined with structural imbalances and rising debt, have made Sisi’s economic policies untenable – even among his allies.

The long-lasting economic crisis is an existential threat to the regime’s stability. Sisi himself may have calculated that Egypt urgently needs a new social contract to avoid economic-driven social unrest that could push him out or plunge the country into perpetual chaos. 

He will likely want to avoid the fate of President Hosni Mubarak, who was forced to leave office amid the January 25 Revolution in 2011. It is also likely that there will be an arrangement to protect Sisi and his family members from potential future prosecutions as a condition of him stepping down. 

Protecting the state 

The second factor relates to Sisi’s vision for his presidency and the state. This is fundamentally shaped by the 2011 uprising, which he has described as ‘the death certificate of the Egyptian state.’ 

Since he was sworn in in 2014, Sisi has repeatedly warned that another popular uprising would threaten the state’s existence. He has portrayed national prosperity as depending on excluding from Egypt’s politics what he frequently calls ‘ahl elshar’ (people of evil), often understood as referring to Islamists. He has also warned of threats to ‘national memory’ on social media. 

Sisi has portrayed it as his – and the military’s – national duty to spare Egypt the chaos engulfing other Arab Spring countries by removing the Muslim Brotherhood from power amid a popular uprising. He has indicated that he considers it his duty to reshape Egypt’s politics to guarantee long-term stability as he sees it.   

In his speech at the military academy, Sisi revealed that he had insisted on incorporating Article 200 into the 2019 constitutional amendments. This article effectively designates the military as the guardian of Egypt’s national, secular identity and the regime. 

Given this, Sisi may therefore feel that departing in 2030 is in line with his aims. The military-trained officials he has designated as his successors would serve as the practical implementers of this vision.

Military-shaped succession

Alongside his plans to step down, Sisi also announced that the armed forces will fund a 30-month military academy course to train potential future leaders. Egyptians will then be able to ‘elect and choose’ from among the graduates.

The course will train select candidates, who must have a PhD and be 40-50 years old, for positions including minister, member of parliament, governor, and potentially even president. Those who have served in government for at least six years will be exempted. 

Sisi’s choice of the military academy is not surprising, since it has long been tasked with promoting a military-centric nationalism and overseeing appointments and promotions in state institutions. This has sometimes sparked resistance, for example from judges in January. 

In effect, the system will replace the electoral process with competence criteria, narrowing the pool of trusted candidates and excluding anyone who is ‘tendentious, a traitor, or a criminal’ from becoming president. 

Future implications

Although this process finally paves the way for civilians to become president, the military will likely retain decisive influence over leadership selection and the state’s strategic direction. The military’s constitutional mandate means its commanders’ views and preferences would continue to shape key state decisions.

Related work

Should Egypt join the Mecca Pact?

In this setup, Sisi will likely retain entrenched loyalties and broader political influence. The changes could establish an informal military guardianship model that sits above the president and government beyond 2030. This might resemble Turkey in the 1990s.

The new government training system might also invite challenges. It seems designed to side-line dissidents, the Muslim Brotherhood and rival generals. But by effectively excluding individuals without a postgraduate degree or those who fail to secure academy approval, it might be deemed unconstitutional and face legal challenges. It could also spark fierce competition among key security branches.

Will Sisi reconsider?

Sisi’s decision to step down might face resistance from key institutions and influential figures in his patronage system, who may try to convince him to reconsider to protect their interests. 

These attempts may intensify if Egypt’s military becomes involved in escalating regional conflicts. Sisi recently sought authorization from parliament to deploy troops to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. 

If living conditions worsen and social unrest breaks out, Sisi may conclude that staying in power best guarantees stability for Egypt. 

Potential for civilian rule?

Despite its risks, Sisi’s decision may facilitate a transition towards a less authoritarian government in the long term. It took Egyptians 15 years after the 2011 uprising to hear an Egyptian president pledge an ordinary, peaceful transition of power. 

By declaring he will step down, Sisi could end up kickstarting a tradition in which no single ruler stays in power until death. Civilians might finally be seen as capable rulers. 

This will not happen overnight, of course. It would depend on Sisi keeping his word and social stability holding until 2030. But if this is the case, the military guardianship Sisi is establishing may, in the long term, be seen as a transitional period toward a more stable, more open and freer society.

item.title: Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine?
item.description:
Will the US midterms change Washington’s policy on Israel and Palestine? Expert comment jon.wallace 22 October 2026

Not immediately. But a Democratic victory could set the terms for a new approach by the next president.

Whatever the results, November’s midterm elections will not immediately transform US policy toward Israel and Palestine. In any outcome, the separation of powers means that President Donald Trump will still control American foreign policy. Even a Democrat-controlled Congress could not compel his administration to pursue a fundamentally different approach. 

But the midterms may accelerate a transformation that is already underway in the Democratic Party and among the US electorate, where the political centre of gravity on Israel and Palestine is shifting rapidly. 

If Democrats win a majority in either or both houses, they will gain new congressional tools to act on Israel–Palestine issues. Most importantly, the legislation they put forward would establish the policy baseline from which a future Democratic administration would govern.

The shift

Among dozens of others, Democrats like Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and Angela Gonzales-Torres, running in the general against another Democrat in California, have drawn considerable attention for their criticism of Israeli government actions – and US support for them. The race in Michigan, which could be decisive for Democratic hopes to retake the senate, looks tight.

But even if progressive candidates don’t do as well as expected in these elections, a shift is underway. Developments in Washington over just the past month illustrate how much has already changed.

On 29 September, 46 of 47 Senate Democrats voted for a resolution led by Senators Chris Van Hollen, Tim Kaine and Bernie Sanders. This would ‘require the Department of State to provide information and assessments related to investigations of the killing of United States citizens by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces in the West Bank’. The resolution did not pass the Republican majority. But the vote was remarkable for its unanimity. Such Democratic unity on a resolution critical of Israel would have been almost unimaginable only a few years ago.

The vote follows a distinct trajectory in Democratic politics. When Senator Bernie Sanders forced the Senate to vote on blocking weapon sales to Israel in November 2024, only 18 Democrat senators supported him. This April, 40 of 47 Senate Democrats voted against a sale of bulldozers to Israel. And 36 opposed the sale of 1,000-pound bombs. Now, with the September resolution, virtually the entire Senate Democratic caucus has voted to demand accountability from Israel.

Then came the House of Representatives. On 1 October, Rep. Joaquin Castro and other members introduced the Stop the Settlements Act. This builds on the Biden administration’s 2024 sanctions on violent Israeli extremists in the West Bank, which saw a major power set up a process to sanction those undermining peace and threatening violence in the West Bank. 

It also builds on the subsequent 2026 sanctions by European countries and Canada against products originating in Israeli settlements. The Act would impose sanctions on individuals and entities responsible for building or expanding Israeli settlements and outposts in the West Bank or Gaza and prohibit settlement goods from entering the US market. 

These developments point toward an emerging Democratic Party position: one that more actively defends the rights of the Palestinian people and is more willing to seek to compel Israel and the White House to move in that direction. Notably, Barack Obama’s planned 24 October event with El-Sayed on the campaign trail shows a greater willingness by the party’s elite to accommodate criticism of Israeli policies.

That shift matters. Israel and Palestine remain secondary issues for most US voters, compared to the economy, healthcare, education and other domestic concerns. But firm convictions on Israel–Palestine have become important attributes for some candidates in Democratic party politics. And the midterms will, in some ways, be a referendum on how criticism of Israeli policies affects voter intentions – with candidates like El-Sayed calling Israeli actions in Gaza a genocide, a claim the Netanyahu government strenuously denies. 

But one thing looks certain: US views on the Israeli government have become less favourable across age groups and political parties. Even among American Jews, 61 per cent believe Israel is guilty of war crimes and 39 per cent call it genocide, according to a 2025 Washington Post poll. The tide may already have decisively shifted, regardless of whether or not candidates like El-Sayed win their races. 

A Democratic Congress

Democratic takeover of the House and the Senate would make the shift more consequential immediately. Much of Congress’s influence over foreign policy occurs not through dramatic floor votes, but through the accumulation of hearings, letters, reporting requirements, funding restrictions and private pressure on administrations. 

Democratic-controlled committees could hold hearings on settlement expansion in the West Bank and settler violence, scrutinize US arms sales to Israel, demand administration briefings, investigate the treatment of American citizens, mark-up legislation and use appropriations and oversight to press the executive branch. 

House and Senate Democrats should begin laying the groundwork to create an affirmative American Palestine policy. That is, a policy not only defined by a move to restrict Israeli settlement-building and the sale of weapons to Israel, but one that advocates for Palestinian self-determination and an architecture for advancing it. 

Over the decades, Congress has constructed a dense web of laws that restrict American relations with the PLO and the Palestinian Authority. A Democratic Congress could therefore begin to map those restrictions and decide how to address them. Which can be addressed administratively? Which need Congressional amendment or repeal? What policy changes will the US seek from the Palestinian leadership? 

This will not be straightforward: Democrats are still debating these policies, and unanimity will not always be possible: there remains a diversity of views and priorities within the party. 

Congress also needs far greater exposure to Palestinian political, economic and civil-society leaders. While many US politicians routinely engage with every dimension of Israeli politics, few have sustained relationships with Palestinians who can explain Palestinian institutions, aspirations and internal debates.

Two time horizons

Were candidates like El-Sayed to lose their races, and were midterms results to be disappointing for the Democrats, it is possible that some in the party might hesitate about the trajectory on Israel and Palestine policy.

But, assuming Democrats gain control of Congress, they could use 2027 and 2028 to constrain, oversee and prepare. A Democratic Congress could press Israel for accountability for violence against Palestinians and Americans, challenge settlement expansion, scrutinize US military assistance, support viable elements of Gaza reconstruction, strengthen Palestinian institutions and begin removing legal obstacles to normal US-Palestinian relations.

These preparations will be significant if a Democrat returns to the White House in 2029. A new administration will be best able to move forward a markedly different policy if significant progress is made in the previous two years.

In this respect, though the midterms will not be the moment US policy toward Israel and Palestine changes, they can set the context for any Democrat running in the presidential primaries – which essentially begin as soon as the new Congress is seated. 

Those who have been advocating for Palestinian rights for decades now see that not only their elected representatives, but the next US president may align with them as well. 

That will not fix anything today for the relatives of the more than 70,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza, the millions that continue to suffer in the occupied territories, or Israelis dealing with the aftermath of the Hamas cross-border attacks of 7 October 2023. But it does provide a modicum of hope that there is a pathway to freedom and liberty for all. What we’ll learn from the US midterms is how quickly that change is likely to come.

item.title: Donald Trump has sold out Ukraine. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
Europe’s leaders can no longer trust a word that comes out of Washington. No more slaps on the wrist – we need concrete steps to punish Trump

Historical comparisons are always inexact. No one conflict precisely mirrors another. Yet Donald Trump’s shameless appeasement of Vladimir Putin carries more than a noxious whiff of Neville Chamberlain’s failed attempt in Munich in 1938 to head off war with Nazi Germany. To be fair to the former UK prime minister – and history largely hasn’t been – his peacemaking efforts had the enthusiastic backing of most people in Britain and France who, like him, were desperate to avoid a repeat of the horrors of the first world war. Trump enjoys no equivalent public support for his treachery. Nor does he face the prospect of a US war with Russia. His betrayal of Ukraine is cynically self-interested, globally dangerous and utterly contemptible.

US-Russian talks on agreeing the shoddy terms of a precedent-setting American sell-out of Ukraine are at an advanced stage, after meetings in St Petersburg this week. Trump has zigzagged over the war ever since returning to office. Now, panicked by record-low poll ratings, he seems determined to scapegoat Ukraine and force its de facto capitulation. Recent steps – his shocking decision to fund Putin’s war machine by buying Russian diesel, his waiving of tougher sanctions, his mysterious, lethal interruptions in US satellite and intelligence sharing with Kyiv, and his renewed attempt to oust Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – mark Trump out as the skulking Judas, the craven Brutus of the modern age. He makes Chamberlain look like a man of iron principle. All that’s lacking is an umbrella.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Hybrid Threats: Why Awareness Must Transcend Individual Cyberattacks
item.description:
Every October, Cybersecurity Awareness Month puts practical security measures in the spotlight. Can an employee recognize a phishing email? Will someone pause before clicking a suspicious link? Are passwords and access credentials being protected? These are important questions; individual behaviors are crucial to maintaining cybersecurity.

But awareness is so laser focused on preventing and mitigating the malicious cyberattack, it’s easy to lose sight of the bigger picture: the cyberattack in front of you may be only one piece of the threat.

In the era of hybrid threats, a cyberattack could be part of a broader campaign in which digital activity intersects with cognitive warfare, sabotage, unusual drone activity, disruptions to communications and navigation systems, and much more. State and state-linked networks might use online fraud or scams to generate revenue for operations, launder funds and undermine confidence in financial and/or government institutions.

The challenge for security and law enforcement agencies transcends detecting and responding to one cyber incident at a time. They must also determine whether events that appear separate may be connected.

That distinction changes what it means to be aware, and the urgency is intensifying. Recent research and reporting shows Russian cyber activity directed at European targets is likely intended to enable intelligence collection, operational reach and long-term access rather than immediate disruption. In parallel, the Iranian government is believed to be relying on a longstanding hybrid warfare model combining cyber operations, asymmetric military operations, information warfare, proxy attacks and coercive state activity, with AI increasingly acting as a force multiplier.

Expect to see more of this going forward, not less.

CONNECTING THE DOTS

Consider the signals individually: a government agency experiences a cyberattack. Unusual drone activity is reported over critical infrastructure. GPS service is disrupted. False or misleading information is deliberately spread. Viewed on their own, these events may have different causes, and each can appear to be a separate incident.

Yet hybrid campaigns often depend on individual activities initially looking ambiguous or unrelated. If each signal is treated only as a self-contained incident, relevant connections may be missed – and when the connections are missed, so is the broader pattern they could form.

This does not make traditional cybersecurity awareness less important. It makes awareness more demanding. The familiar focus on individual judgment must be matched by institutional awareness: the ability of government agencies, armed forces, critical infrastructure operators, and other relevant organizations to recognize which signals may matter beyond the immediate event.

That begins before advanced analysis enters the picture. An organization cannot share information it did not capture, and it cannot capture information it did not recognize as potentially relevant. The first requirement is therefore a common understanding of what may be security-relevant and what information is needed to contribute to a broader situational picture.

This shift is central to the awareness challenge. A suspicious link has a clear place in the traditional conversation. A weak signal in a hybrid environment may not have the same clarity. Its significance may emerge only when it is considered alongside other information. Awareness, in this context, means looking beyond the apparent boundaries of a single incident without assuming that any one event tells the entire story.

The sequence matters: recognize, capture, share, assess. If a potentially relevant signal drops out at any stage, it cannot inform the larger picture. If it moves through that sequence, it becomes one piece of information that can be examined in relation to others.

The next task is to bring those fragmented pieces together. Threat intelligence, decision intelligence and artificial intelligence can help teams work across large volumes of data, correlate information, reveal connections, and alert analysts to anomalies. Their value is especially clear when no single signal is decisive. Several weak and seemingly unrelated signals may form a pattern that supports a more informed assessment of the security situation.

The point is not simply to accumulate more data. It is to make relevant information usable as part of a coherent view. A list of isolated incidents still leaves decision-makers looking at fragments. A situational picture asks a different set of questions: What may connect these events? What does the combined pattern suggest? Which developments deserve closer attention? And what might happen next?

That last question is essential. The goal is not limited to identifying a cyberattack or another security-relevant event after it occurs. It is to understand the relationships among relevant signals well enough to identify potential future developments at an early stage. Detection remains necessary, but detection without connection can leave the larger threat out of view.

For Cybersecurity Awareness Month, this broader perspective offers a useful way to expand the conversation. At the individual level, awareness still means recognizing the suspicious email, protecting credentials, avoiding scams and frauds and thinking before clicking. At the national level, it also means making sure the right organizations know what to notice, what to record, what to share, and how to place that information in context.

The difference is one of scale. An individual may be watching for a malicious link. Government agencies, armed forces, critical infrastructure operators, and other relevant organizations must also be watching for relationships among cyber activity, disinformation, sabotage, drone activity and communications interference.

That is the blind spot Cybersecurity Awareness Month should help bring into focus. There’s more to awareness than paying attention before clicking a link. Awareness means we know which signals deserve attention, whether we can bring them together, and whether we can see the threat they may form before the pattern becomes unmistakable.

Critical minerals: The UK’s role in securing resilient supply chains 5 November 2026 — 12:00 TO 13:30 GMT Anonymous (not verified) 22 October 2026 Chatham House and Online

Hear from the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee as it launches its report on how the UK can build resilient critical minerals supply chains, alongside like-minded partners.

Hear from the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee as it launches its report on how the UK can build resilient critical minerals supply chains, alongside like-minded partners.

Critical minerals have moved from the margins of industrial policy to the centre of economic and national security strategy. As demand accelerates and geopolitical competition intensifies, governments face a shared challenge: how to build supply chains that are resilient, responsible and commercially viable. For the UK, the question is not only how to secure access, but also how to draw on its strengths in finance, markets and international partnerships to help shape the next generation of global supply chains.

This event brings together members of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, practitioners and policymakers to launch the Committee’s report on critical minerals, unpack their findings, and explore the dilemmas and opportunities facing the UK.

This event discusses:

  • Why have critical minerals become central to economic and national security strategy?
  • What will be required to meet the needs of both the energy transition and future defence capabilities?
  • How can governments build supply chains that are resilient, responsible and commercially viable?
  • How can the UK draw on its strengths in finance, markets and international partnerships to shape the next generation of global supply chains?
  • What role can like-minded nations play in creating durable mineral ecosystems?
  • Where should UK policymakers and industry focus as demand accelerates and competition intensifies?

The discussion will be followed by half an hour of coffee and networking.

item.title: Slouching toward Kaliningrad, NATO dismisses a nuclear threat
item.description:
During the Cold War, the exclave of West Berlin, isolated in the middle of Communist East Germany, was regarded as one of the most dangerous potential flashpoints for a conflict between the Soviet Union and the West. Indeed, Joseph Stalin’s blockade of land access to the city in 1948-49 came close to triggering a new war, until the U.S. and Britain proved able to supply the population by air.

It is a pity, if not altogether surprising, that Western leaders gave no thought to this history before extending NATO membership to Poland and Lithuania, thereby isolating the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad (Koenigsberg in the former German East Prussia) behind NATO lines.

It is now common for Western security analysts to describe the “Suwalki Gap” in northeast Poland, situated between Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus, as the most dangerous point in the growing Russia-NATO confrontation. Yet they carefully omit to recall that it was NATO, not Russia, that made it so.

The acute strategic vulnerability of Kaliningrad is one key reason why growing fears that Russia may “test NATO” by seizing the Estonian town of Narva, on the Russian border, are so absurd. For one inevitable result of a Russian invasion of NATO territory would be a NATO blockade of Kaliningrad by land and sea. As a Russian security expert remarked to me, “Does anyone in the West seriously believe that Putin or any other Russian leader would risk losing Kaliningrad for the sake of gaining Narva, or having to launch a nuclear war in order to save it?”

Or as former Latvian Defense Minister Artis Pabriks has undiplomatically but accurately stated, "We have always assumed that, if such a war were to break out, Russia would cut off the Suwałki Corridor. But somehow we don’t consider the possibility that, if Russia were to attack, [Kaliningrad] would be the first to be overrun [by NATO forces]. And then there would be no Suwałki Corridor left."

Kaliningrad is the headquarters of the Russian Baltic Fleet and a base for Russian medium-range nuclear missiles. It is also internationally-recognized Russian territory. In U.S. terms, it is as if Pearl Harbor found itself isolated in the middle of Chinese-controlled territory. The progressive expansion of NATO since 1989 to East Germany, Poland, the Baltic States, Sweden and Finland has also turned the Baltic Sea into a NATO lake, with Moscow’s control reduced from the whole eastern and southern shores that it controlled during the Cold War to just Kaliningrad and St. Petersburg.

President Vladimir Putin and the Russian government have stated recently that if NATO blockades Kaliningrad, Russia will respond with nuclear weapons if necessary; every member of the Russian establishment with whom I have spoken has said the same. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, displaying the smirking, strutting frivolity that he has made his trademark, responded that he does “not take this seriously.”

But this threat is serious. Moscow would regard a NATO blockade as a direct act of war. Equally important, with most of the Russian army bogged down in Ukraine, Russia lacks the conventional military force to ensure it can hold Kaliningrad against ground assault or to attack from Belarus, defeat the Polish army and break a siege. Before the invasion of Ukraine, the Russian 11th Army Corps, based in Kaliningrad, had a nominal strength of 12,000 to 18,000 men, backed up by a brigade of naval infantry, but a good many of these troops are reported to have been deployed to Ukraine and lost there. The Polish army has 100,000 men under arms plus 40,000 reservists and is rapidly building up its firepower.

As the U.S Center for Naval Analyses asks, “Kaliningrad: Impregnable Fortress or Russian Alamo?” The consensus among members of the Russian establishment with whom I have spoken is therefore that, in the event of a NATO blockade, Russia would have to issue a nuclear ultimatum immediately and carry the threat through within days if NATO did not back down.

It may seem that NATO countries could not possibly be so crazy as to run the appalling risks involved in imposing a blockade on Kaliningrad; but in fact they have twice suggested moves in this direction. In June 2022, Lithuania announced that (in violation of a previous agreement with Russia) it would impose a ban on the transit to Kaliningrad of goods subject to European Union sanctions, including oil, coal, metals, construction materials and advanced technology — around half of the exclave’s import needs, according to the provincial government of Kaliningrad. After harsh Russian threats of retaliation, the EU backed down and declared that the sanctions would not apply to rail transport.

In June 2025, Sweden announced that it would carry out checks on ships belonging to Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” not only in Swedish territorial waters, but in Sweden’s maritime economic zone. Together with those of the three Baltic States, this covers the whole of the Central Baltic, meaning that the Swedish announcement threatened to blockade St Petersburg and isolate Kaliningrad by sea.

The Swedes and Balts quietly backed down after Russian threats of military intervention to protect the ships and the dispatch of a Russian fighter plane to deter an Estonian patrol boat from boarding a tanker. It is hardly surprising, however, that Moscow is acutely neuralgic about the possibility that this strategy might be resumed.

Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski stated only last month that, “We should not be thinking about our confrontation with Russia only as being confined to Ukraine.

“I was in Latvia just three days ago on a Polish base, we have a tank company there, and … there are no troops on the other side. We closely monitor, as you may imagine, the Kaliningrad exclave. There are hardly any troops there,” Sikorski said. “I’m suggesting we should exercise so aggressively on our side as to make … [Putin] uncertain of what we will do, and so that he needs to draw forces away from Ukraine.”

The ironic thing about this statement is that at the very same time that Sikorski was saying Russia is so weak in the Baltic region that NATO can threaten it with impunity, other Polish officials were warning of the likelihood of an impending Russian attack on NATO to “test” the alliance.

Given the blind recklessness and irresponsibility of such statements and moves, it is therefore just as well that Russia has made absolutely clear what the consequences will be if NATO countries were to put these threats into effect.

It is common for Western analysts to dismiss such Russian fears either as “paranoia” or the result of deliberate manipulation by the Russian government; but a moment’s reflection on their own attitudes should bring them to an awareness of the falsity and hypocrisy of this charge.

A U.S. security establishment that goes into hysterics when a Chinese balloon flies over America is in no position to accuse anyone else of paranoia, and nor are European security figures who allow a few minor acts of arson to spook them into declaring that “we are already at war with Russia.” If the West blockades Kaliningrad, they may learn what a real war with Russia is like.

In old allegorical paintings of Prudence, she is often portrayed holding a mirror. This symbolizes her capacity for self-awareness and self-examination, that in turn leads her to modesty and a better understanding of others. For all our sakes, it would be better if European governments spent less time shouting in Russia’s face and more time examining their own.

item.title: Pulling back to the Second Island Chain would be strategic folly
item.description:
In a recent report, Jennifer Kavanagh of Defense Priorities called for the U.S. to end its formal security commitments to Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines and to withdraw nearly all of its forces in those countries to the Second Island Chain. This shift, Kavanagh argues, would leave the U.S. “more secure” with a “more sustainable military footprint.”

The report deserves credit for diversifying debate in Washington. However, we disagree with Kavanagh’s recommendations. A Second Island Chain strategy would not protect vital U.S. interests or enhance regional stability. U.S. regional dominance, as the report identifies, is no longer possible or necessary, but withdrawing to the Second Island Chain risks destabilizing the region and undermining Washington’s hand in any future conflicts in East Asia.

The geopolitical dimension


The report assumes that after terminating its alliances with Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines, the U.S. could still preserve enough influence in Asia to maintain a balance of power not dominated by China; even without U.S. defense commitments, these allies could not only defend themselves militarily against China but could also retain sufficient political autonomy.

Yet China need not achieve regional dominance through military conquest to render these states exceedingly vulnerable to coercion. Indeed, China can pursue sustained coercion by exploiting economic dependencies or using gray-zone military activities to punish Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines for refusing to accommodate its interests, incentivizing them to bandwagon with China rather than balance against it. Without the U.S. as a credible guarantor for these states’ security, China could, for instance, pressure countries to accommodate its positions in territorial disputes or limit cooperation with the U.S. in strategically important industries like semiconductors and shipbuilding.

U.S. defense commitments in East Asia do not prevent China from engaging in aggressive gray-zone coercion against U.S. allies, as in the South China Sea, but they do raise the costs to China of crossing certain escalatory thresholds. A binding U.S. security guarantee, combined with a credible military deterrent, is an essential backstop to ensure both Chinese and allied activities remain bounded by an appropriate understanding of risk. Without U.S. commitments, China would face far fewer risks in using escalation coercively. Contrary to the report's claims, informal security partnerships and a residual U.S. presence would not provide effective assurances against this risk of coercion.

In light of that reality, it is quite possible that South Korea and Japan would pursue nuclear weapons. Kavanagh acknowledges the risk of regional nuclear proliferation but understates both the likelihood and the dangers associated with it.

In South Korea, there is widespread public support — 76%, as of May 2025 — for an indigenous nuclear deterrent. Though South Korean policymakers are more cautious, a 2024 study found that the majority of South Korean strategic elites who oppose nuclearization would shift their support in favor if Washington terminated its alliance with Seoul. In Japan, despite a strong taboo against nuclear weapons, studies have similarly shown how that reservation erodes when respondents are presented with a world in which the U.S. no longer guarantees Japanese security.

The South Korean and Japanese pursuit of nuclear weapons could plunge East Asia into conflict. Indeed, China and North Korea would face a strong temptation to preempt South Korean or Japanese nuclear development with military force, despite the associated risks. North Korea, in particular, would treat South Korea’s nuclear acquisition as an existential crisis, facing the potential loss of its only military advantage over the South. Japan faces similar risks; China’s insecurity about Japanese rearmament is deep-rooted.

If a conflict were to erupt in Asia, the U.S. could not simply ignore it, even if Washington chose not to intervene militarily. The war would have a direct and severe negative impact on vital U.S. interests, particularly economic ones. Japan and South Korea are the world’s 4th and 12th largest economies and the 6th and 7th largest U.S. trading partners, respectively. Sixty percent of all global trade passes through Asian waters. Bloomberg Economics found that a Second Korean War would cost the world economy 3.9% of GDP — and shrink U.S. GDP by 2.3% — in its first year.

It is unclear why the U.S. would willingly fuel these dangers when the consequences are so severe and, ultimately, avoidable. China does have strong economic and political incentives to pursue stability rather than disruption. But basing U.S. access to the world’s most important region on the hope that Chinese intentions remain status-quo oriented is not a prudent management of risk.

The military dimension


Kavanagh argues that two U.S. interests necessitate a continued but minimal U.S. military presence in East Asia: preventing an attack against the U.S. homeland and maintaining access to the region’s economic markets and trade routes. By Kavanagh’s own definition, therefore, the U.S. should act in some cases against possible Chinese military use in East Asia. The problem, however, is that in the event of a U.S.-China conflict, the U.S. could not secure access to the western Pacific with the majority of its forces deployed to the Second Island Chain rather than the First.

The U.S. must maintain peacetime access to ensure wartime access. Withdrawal would force the U.S. to fight two battles: the fight for access and the conflict itself. Militarily, therefore, no alternative exists to a First Island Chain-centered defense strategy. This holds for two different scenarios: a Chinese amphibious assault and a sea denial campaign.

Why is this the case?

First, China’s land-based anti-access/area-denial capabilities are extensive. Those capabilities are designed specifically to counter U.S. power projection in the region. U.S. forces are most vulnerable when they are massed and operating in the open — easy targets for China’s long-range, precision-strike missiles, which can reach well into the Second Island Chain. Defending against a Chinese amphibious assault in the First Island Chain from the Second would require U.S. forces to surge forward across thousands of miles of exposed, open ocean for weeks at a time.

Second, the U.S. lacks the required sealift to rapidly move the bulk of its combat power forward in a conflict. A 2019 Department of Defense exercise found that only about 40% of U.S. sealift was ready for immediate use in a crisis. Similarly, Adm. Samuel Paparo, head of U.S. Pacific Command, has said his command’s Combat Logistics Force, which includes sea and airlift, only meets 60% of current operational requirements.

Third, China possesses the world’s largest navy by hull count, and it is becoming increasingly proficient at operating its fleet at sea for weeks at a time, including in the Second Island Chain. The U.S. can no longer assume, as Kavanagh appears to do, that it will enjoy an uncontested command of the sea. Instead, the U.S. and China will compete intensely for sea control. In the event of a Chinese sea denial campaign, withdrawing to the Second Island Chain would put the U.S. at a severe operational disadvantage. It would make it far easier for China’s surface ships — nearly all of which are armed with anti-ship missiles — and submarines to prevent the U.S. from gaining access to and operating in the western Pacific. Any plausible effort to re-secure trade routes would require, at minimum, a months-long naval campaign with a level of attrition unseen since the Second World War.

Willingly choosing to respond to a conflict from the Second Island Chain would thus provide China an extraordinary advantage. Five thousand U.S. forces in Japan, which Kavanagh would like to reduce even further by 2035, would serve as little more than a speedbump. China would begin a conflict on third base, while the U.S. would be forced to sit at first and fight its way to second. A Second Island Chain strategy would therefore not reduce U.S. forces’ vulnerability or casualties; it would likely increase both, and unnecessarily.

Of course, Kavanagh bases part of her argument on the assumption that reductions in U.S. forces in the First Island Chain will obviate the very reason for their use by reducing Chinese threat perceptions and thus the risk of an unnecessary war. Yet that assumption is misplaced. Changes to U.S. and Chinese force posture in the region are not the primary source of tension between the two countries; rather, their political differences are. Military tensions are simply a byproduct of that competition. It is thus unlikely that withdrawing to the Second Island Chain would fundamentally mitigate U.S.-China hostility. As made clear above, a Second Island Chain strategy would not serve as a sufficient hedge if assumptions about moderate Chinese intent proved inaccurate.

None of this means that the U.S. should continue on its current policy course in East Asia. Its relationship with China requires delicate diplomatic management, and cooperation should be pursued where possible. The U.S. should seek healthy competition, not one of unnecessary hostility. As recent research has called for, Washington should work to achieve constructive strategic stability with Beijing.

Further, while a First Island Chain defense strategy enables intervention to defend Taiwan, it does not necessitate it. Formal U.S. treaty allies should remain the principal focus of U.S. defense efforts. Making that clear would go a long way in helping reduce U.S.-China tensions. The US should stay out of Saudi Arabia’s war
item.description:
After a four year truce, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have returned to open conflict in Yemen.

Last month, the Saudis conducted over 250 air raids that killed over 150 civilians according to the Yemen Data Project, while the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, relied on drone and missile attacks targeting Saudi oil infrastructure and more recently civilian airports, in attacks that killed 14 people.

A growing Saudi-led coalition to defeat the Houthis is coalescing, but at this point President Donald Trump has resisted requests from Saudi Arabia to resume airstrikes on Yemen, following the truce he concluded with the Houthis in May 2025. That’s not to say the U.S. is staying on the sidelines, of course; Washington has already sent 200 military and intelligence advisors to assist the Saudis.

Mainstream coverage of further U.S. intervention largely misses the critical and concerning context of America joining yet another war against the Houthis: the last Saudi-led coalition war led to one of the worst humanitarian crises in modern history, aggravated by numerous alleged Saudi war crimes. And neither that campaign nor Washington’s recent standoff with the Houthis did much of anything to slow the group’s advances in Yemen.

So why would we join Saudi Arabia in this war — and why do we treat them as a valued ally in the first place?

These are the questions we posed to Quincy Institute Middle East research fellow Annelle Sheline in the latest episode of Always at War.

Sheline has worked closely on Yemen and is intimately familiar with America's human rights record, having worked in the State Department’s Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor before resigning in March 2024 over America’s blind support for Israel’s war in Gaza.

We asked her about her time at the State Department and why the human rights reports, meant to help enforce rules like the Leahy Law, are so often ignored. What we learned is just how easy it is for these reports to be used to start wars but almost never to end them.

As Sheline put it, human rights reports may be cited as an excuse to hammer U.S. adversaries but are often overlooked or conveniently forgotten when it comes to imposing consequences on U.S. allies, like withholding military support following alleged war crimes. At the same time Annelle’s bureau awarded small pockets of money to journalists or civil society groups working on human rights, the U.S. was sending massive amounts of security assistance to authoritarian governments that kill journalists, like Saudi Arabia.

For Sheline, the math is simple: the U.S. should stay out of Saudi Arabia’s war. The Houthis have repeatedly thwarted U.S. efforts to destroy them, so why try again and risk another disastrous humanitarian crisis? If anything, Sheline believes we ought to push the Saudis toward a negotiated truce, because history has already shown that there is no military solution to Yemen’s profound political crisis.

After all, if America is ever going to end its cycle of permanent war, it’s going to require breaking from the dismal logic of U.S. interventionism that underscored the last decade of Yemen policy — a failing approach that a doddering Joe Biden summarized succinctly late in his term: “Are [US airstrikes] stopping the Houthis? No. Are they gonna continue? Yes.”

item.title: Meeting Arctic security threats: Do Europe’s new strategies make sense?
item.description:
Meeting Arctic security threats: Do Europe’s new strategies make sense? Expert comment jon.wallace 22 October 2026

Responding to security threats from Russian military capabilities and increasing Chinese activity are largely sensible. But a lack of alignment on climate policy risk undermining the security they seek to strengthen.

September’s security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark has, for the time being, lowered the political temperature in the High North following months of tension over US ambitions towards Greenland. But the Arctic is being reshaped by multiple converging factors.

Accelerating climate change and ecosystem degradation are intersecting with geopolitical tensions, military activity, and competition for resources to make the region increasingly important. Arctic sea lanes, long considered unviable, are drawing interest following disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea – though they are still not reliably ice-free.

In response, the UK published its updated Arctic Policy Framework on 15 October, swiftly followed by the EU’s own updated strategy for the Arctic ‘Europe’s Northern Neighbourhood’ on 20 October.

Both documents make important moves on enhancing military preparedness in the region. But alongside strategies for securing an Arctic that is melting, greater efforts are needed to keep it frozen.

From ‘low tensions’ to hard security

There are differences between the UK and EU strategies: The UK’s framework declares that the ‘High North, Low Tension’ policy followed by Arctic countries for 30 years is effectively over and adopts a NATO-first approach, based on deterrence and warfighting readiness. The EU’s strategy prioritizes maritime surveillance, military mobility and protection of subsea infrastructure, creating ‘dual-use and multi-purpose capabilities’ – placing the Arctic into the broader agenda of EU ‘Strategic Autonomy’.

Related work

Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying

But both strategies recognize the importance of the Arctic for security, and the need to respond to a greater Russian and Chinese presence in the region. 

The threat is real. Over the last decade, Russia has established a new Arctic command and new Arctic military bases. Russia also has a long history of conducting military and intelligence operations under the cover of its Arctic and maritime research outfits. And communication lines between NATO and Russian forces in the region have effectively collapsed since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

China, meanwhile, claims to be a near Arctic state, and has shared plans for a new class of container ships, developed with Russia, to navigate the Northern Sea Route, which skirts Russia’s coast. Fears that this route may become a new trade chokepoint are probably overblown, while volumes are so low. But Moscow and Beijing are increasing military cooperation in the Arctic, for instance through joint air and sea patrols. 

NATO activities have intensified in return. Sweden and Finland have joined the alliance, increasing the number of member-states with Arctic territory. And over the last decade, the UK has expanded its cooperation with Nordic NATO members, through the Joint Expeditionary Force established in 2014, increased training alongside Norwegian armed forces, and a joint frigate procurement programme with Oslo announced in 2025. In January, the Royal Marines deployment to Norway was expanded to a year-round commitment. 

The new UK Arctic Strategy focuses on further strengthening deterrence and interoperability with NATO partners and commits to doubling the number of British troops training in Norway to 2,000 by 2029. 

That signals a significant shift in the UK’s attention to Northern Europe. And it places the UK’s Arctic military activities in the context of its greater presence in the ‘Wider North’, building on long-standing commitments to air policing over Iceland, maritime patrols and under-ice submarine deployments, and recent NATO initiatives like Arctic and Baltic Sentry. It also emphasizes the UK’s reorientation to Europe in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review. 

Both strategies also highlight the need for good governance. But this will likely be a struggle. The Arctic Council, a post-Cold War governance initiative that convenes all states and indigenous communities in Arctic territory, worked reasonably well for most of the post-1991 period. But Russia was excluded from the Council following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, creating another international forum undermined by the war.

Climate change remains central challenge for Arctic security

Both the UK and EU strategies recognize climate change as a central challenge in the Arctic. They link the urgency of tackling the climate crisis to achieving net zero and emphasize the need to better understand climate tipping points. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

However, the strategies could be more explicit about what crossing these tipping points could mean for the UK and Europe – particularly the increasing likelihood of Greenland ice sheet collapse and further weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). That would pose a severe threat and cascading pressures to Europe’s food security, infrastructure, public finances and resilience. This threat makes protecting the Arctic from climate change a core European security interest.

The UK and EU strategies also need to draw stronger connections between Arctic climate research, domestic preparedness and international leadership on climate mitigation to help advance solutions and practical protection against these risks.

Halting global warming and preserving Arctic ice should be recognized as essential parts of a security strategy. Stronger climate action today could reduce, or even prevent, some of the geopolitical tensions and security risks associated with a warming Arctic. A rapidly melting Arctic increases the risk of new maritime disputes, conflicts over critical minerals, more pollution from shipping, environmental damage from new infrastructure development and uncontrolled extractive industrial activity.

Both updated strategies face unresolved policy tensions between protecting the region from climate impacts, pursuing new economic opportunities and expanding the European security presence. 

For instance, increasing exploration for resources – as both strategies advocate – could mean creating significant new infrastructure to extract and export. That risks increasing emissions and heaping further pressure on the Arctic’s fragile ecosystems. 

Meanwhile, constructing new dual-use infrastructure, as proposed by the EU strategy, may support civilian services, scientific research and emergency preparedness. But its military functions could fuel securitization of the Arctic.

On critical minerals, the UK’s strategy makes clear it will not sponsor or support the issuance of deep-sea mining exploitation contracts that conflict with the International Seabed Authority’s Mining Code, which regulates prospecting, exploration and exploitation of marine minerals. This is an important message, because it affirms that competition for critical minerals must remain subject to multilateral governance and international rules.  

Success depends on strong Arctic partnerships 

For their strategies to succeed, the UK and EU will need to deepen cooperation with Arctic states and communities, building on their generally welcomed security roles and the significant contribution of UK science to Arctic climate research. At the same time, the UK and EU need to remain sensitive to growing apprehension in the region about the motivations of non-Arctic actors.

Despite geopolitical tensions, there have been positive developments in Arctic governance. Greenland’s prominent role in negotiating the recent US security agreement signals a shift towards greater agency in decisions historically dominated by external powers. 

The UK and EU should support this shift by strengthening indigenous participation in decisions affecting Arctic security and economic development, through institutions such as the Inuit Circumpolar Council and Saami Council. That will advance an approach to Arctic security that encompasses climate, food, health, livelihoods and cultural continuity alongside military concerns. 

More comprehensive Arctic strategies are clearly needed. And the updated strategies largely make sense. Yet, managing the trade-offs between defence, economic development, climate protection and indigenous rights requires careful policy design, clearer priorities and meaningful engagement with Arctic communities. 

Finally, the US will remain central to Arctic security. That makes sustained transatlantic engagement essential. Europe has demonstrated that, when united and working in cooperation with Canada, they can influence US policy towards the Arctic. Building on that collective strength can help ensure that future cooperation strengthens security across all dimensions.
